findings.message: This change removes 114's allow-list and puts a deny-list in its place. The goal is that each log line stays one line. The deny-list covers C0 controls, DEL, U+2028 and U+2029. It misses U+0085 (NEL), which Unicode treats as a mandatory line break, and the rest of the C1 controls (U+0080–U+009F). Before this change, 114's `[^\w.:-]` replaced all of them. Callers put text they don't control into the scope, for example `` `ai.tool ${call.name}` `` (a tool name the model picks) and `` `delivery.ingest ${t.key} ${t.task}` ``. Fix: add `\x80-\x9f` to the character class, i.e. `/[\p{Zl}\p{Zp}\x00-\x1f\x7f-\x9f]/gu`. The `\n\r` entries are already inside `\x00-\x1f`. Add a U+0085 row to the 115 test table.
findings.scenario: Before this change, `logError("chat\u0085amax admin: Error [00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000000]", new Error("x"))` wrote `_`. Now it writes a raw NEL. A log viewer or pipeline that breaks lines on Unicode newlines shows a second, forged line starting `amax admin: Error [...]`.

findings.message: The comment on line 6 of log.ts says DEL, U+2029 and the error-name path are covered. The 115 variant table tests none of them: it checks the scope only, with CR/LF, a tab and U+2028. Add rows for U+2029 and DEL (0x7f), and one row that puts a control character in the error's name, so the new expression is pinned for every kind it claims to handle.
findings.scenario: If `\p{Zp}` or `\x7f` were dropped from the regex, every test would still pass.
